messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Amara's Story

Amara was twenty-three when the fighting reached the clinic in Mogadishu where she worked as a nurse. She had trained in Lagos and moved to Somalia two years earlier, drawn by a sense of purpose and a belief that her skills could matter in a place where they were desperately needed. The clinic was a converted school building with concrete walls and a generator that ran on fuel they rationed carefully. On the morning of the attack, she was changing dressings on a patient with a leg wound when the first explosion came—close enough that dust fell from the ceiling and the lights flickered. Within minutes, the clinic flooded with casualties. People arrived bleeding, calling out, some barely conscious. Amara moved between them, her hands steady, her mind focused on triage and what she could do. Then a man was brought in with shrapnel embedded in his abdomen and chest. She was cleaning around the wounds when he seized, his body convulsing against the stretcher. She called for help, but there was no surgeon, no operating theatre, nothing but her hands and gauze and the absolute certainty that he was dying in front of her and she could not stop it. He died within minutes. She could not remember his name, only the heat of his body and the sound of his breathing stopping.

That was two years ago. Amara is twenty-five now and lives in Boston with her boyfriend Marcus, who she met six months after returning home. On the surface, her life looks stable. She works the night shift at a teaching hospital, a position that suits her—fewer people around, quieter wards, time to think. But the thinking is what undoes her. When she is alone in the early hours, changing a patient's IV or documenting vitals, a smell or a sound will pull her back to that room in Mogadishu, and the memory arrives not as something she recalls but as something happening now. Her hands shake. Her heart races. The man's face—she can see it clearly even though she could not have seen it clearly then—becomes vivid and immediate. The feeling of helplessness floods through her body as if she is standing at that stretcher again, unable to save him. When the memory takes hold, she feels overwhelmed by an emotion so vast and so heavy that she has to stop what she is doing, has to step away from the patient she is tending. Sometimes it is grief, pure and suffocating; sometimes it is something closer to panic. Either way, she cannot stay present.

What frightens Amara most, though, is not the memory itself but what the memory means about her. She had come to believe that a competent nurse—a good nurse—would have found a way. She would have known what to do, would have been resourceful enough, brave enough, skilled enough to prevent that death. The fact that she could not means something is fundamentally wrong with her. She is inadequate. She feels permanently humiliated by her failure, as though everyone who looks at her can see the defect underneath. This belief has become so solid that she cannot imagine anyone understanding if she tried to explain what happened. She has not talked to Marcus about the details, though he knows she was in a war zone and that it was hard. The thought of speaking about it aloud—of saying the words that would make it real to someone else—fills her with a shame so acute that she pushes the thought away. Instead, she has learned to retreat inward. When the memory threatens, when the weight of her inadequacy becomes unbearable, she drifts into a kind of fantasy escape, a mental space where she is someone else, somewhere else, someone who did not fail. She imagines herself as a surgeon in a fully equipped hospital in London, or a researcher working in a quiet lab. She spends hours in these fantasies, especially on her days off, and they are a relief—a few hours where she does not feel the weight of being defective, where the memory cannot touch her.

But the fantasies only work while she is alone and still. Once the shift begins, once she is actually working, the fantasies collapse. She finds herself back in the present, back in her body, and the memories are waiting. She has started to avoid thinking about the event deliberately, pushing away any thought that might lead her back there. Yet the avoidance itself has become a trigger. When she tries not to think about something, the effort of suppression only makes the memory more insistent, more vivid. She will be standing at a medication cart and suddenly see his face. She will be explaining a procedure to a patient and feel the wave of grief coming. And each time it happens, each time the memory overwhelms her despite her efforts to keep it at bay, it confirms what she already believes: that she is broken, that there is something fundamentally wrong with her capacity to function, that she should have been able to prevent this and could not. The memory and the shame feed each other in a cycle she cannot break. Marcus has noticed that she is distant, that she seems to leave the room sometimes even when she is standing right there. He has asked her twice if she wants to talk to someone. She has said no both times, but the second time she said it, she meant it less. What she is most afraid of now is that if she stops escaping—if she stops the fantasies, if she stops avoiding the thoughts—the memory will consume her entirely. But what she is also beginning to suspect, in the quiet moments before her shifts, is that the escape and avoidance are consuming her anyway, just more slowly.
